MHHS2401 · Week 3 · Muscle Physiology I — Dr Linda Ban

Muscle Excitation & Contraction structure, the NMJ, and the sliding-filament mechanism

The full chain from molecule to movement — how skeletal muscle is built, how a nerve switches it on at the neuromuscular junction, and how calcium and ATP drive the sliding-filament contraction and relaxation. Every slide decoded, with the drug, toxin and disease angles.

§0Orientation

From molecule to movement

Three questions in order: what is muscle built from, how is it switched on, and how does it shorten?

This lecture is a chain of cause and effect, so the order matters. First the structure (LO1) — because you cannot follow the contraction machinery without knowing the parts. Then the neuromuscular junction (LO2) — the switch that turns a nerve signal into a muscle signal. Finally the sliding-filament mechanism (LO3) — how the switched-on muscle actually pulls. Of the three muscle types (Plate 0.1), this is all about skeletal muscle: striated, multinucleate and under voluntary control.

Label Key — Muscle types
Skeletal muscle
Striated, multinucleate, voluntary; moves the skeleton — the subject of this lecture.
Cardiac muscle
Striated, branched, involuntary, joined by intercalated discs; only in the heart.
Smooth muscle
Non-striated, single nucleus, involuntary; lines vessels and hollow organs.
Reasoning · why we start with structure

Every step of contraction — calcium flooding out of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, myosin heads walking along actin, the sarcomere shortening — is named after a structural part. Learn the parts first (§1) and the mechanism (§3) becomes a story you can narrate rather than a list to memorise. That is why this guide, like the lecture, refuses to explain contraction until the scaffold is built.

R Recall checklist — orientation
  • The lecture runs structure → NMJ → contraction — each step depends on the last.
  • Skeletal muscle: striated, multinucleate, voluntary (vs cardiac and smooth).
  • Three learning objectives: describe muscle structure; identify the NMJ + its modulation; summarise contraction & relaxation.
§1Structure & properties · LO1

The structure of skeletal muscle

Zoom in four times: muscle → fibre → myofibril → sarcomere.

Skeletal muscle is built as a set of nested bundles. Each level is wrapped in its own connective-tissue sheath, and the wrapping is what gives the whole organ its strength and its route for nerves and vessels.

§1.1One muscle — the connective-tissue sheaths

A whole muscle contains bundles of muscle fibres (fascicles) plus its neurovasculature, held together by three layers of connective tissue (Plate 1.1).

Label Key — Whole-muscle organisation
Epimysium
Wraps the whole muscle — the outermost sheath; continuous with the tendon.
Perimysium
Wraps each fascicle (bundle of fibres); carries the larger nerves and vessels.
Endomysium
Wraps each individual muscle fibre; carries capillaries and the fine nerve endings.
Fascicle
A bundle of muscle fibres — the unit you can see with the naked eye in meat 'grain'.
Muscle fibre
A single muscle cell (myocyte).
Nerve & blood vessels
Run in the connective tissue to reach every fibre.
Reasoning · why three separate wrappings

The sheaths do two jobs at once. Mechanically, they let each fibre and fascicle glide a little independently yet transmit their combined pull to the tendon (all three layers merge into it) — so force is pooled without the fibres shearing each other apart. Logistically, they are the scaffold and the roadways: nerves and capillaries travel along the perimysium and endomysium to reach cells buried deep in the muscle.

Memory hook · epi/peri/endo

Epi = around the entire muscle · Peri = around the packets (fascicles) · Endo = around the individual fibre. Outside-in, biggest to smallest.

§1.2One cell — the muscle fibre

A muscle fibre is a single cell packed with bundles of contractile proteins (myofibrils) plus the machinery to excite them and fuel them (Plate 1.2).

Label Key — Muscle-fibre interior
Myofibrils
Bundles of the contractile proteins; fill most of the cell.
Transverse (T) tubules
In-foldings of the sarcolemma (cell membrane) that carry the action potential into the fibre, deep toward the SR.
Sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR)
Modified endoplasmic reticulum wrapping each myofibril; the cell's calcium store.
Mitochondria & glycogen
The energy supply — ATP and stored fuel for contraction.
Reasoning · why the membrane dives inward as T-tubules

A surface-only action potential would reach the outermost myofibrils long before the core, and the fibre would contract unevenly. The T-tubules carry the signal deep into the cell so the whole cross-section is triggered almost simultaneously — the anatomical trick that makes a fibre contract as one. They also place the membrane right next to the SR's calcium store, setting up the trigger in §3.1.

§1.3One myofibril — the sarcomere and its bands

Each myofibril is a chain of sarcomeres — the contractile units — laid end to end between Z discs (Plate 1.3). The overlap of thick (myosin) and thin (actin) filaments creates the striped 'striated' bands.

Label Key — Sarcomere bands
Sarcomere
The contractile unit, running Z disc to Z disc; sarcomeres sit in series along the myofibril.
Z disc
Anchors actin; marks the edge of each sarcomere.
M line
Anchors myosin; sits at the middle of the sarcomere.
A band
Where myosin and actin overlap — the full length of the thick filament (dark band).
H zone
Myosin only — the central part of the A band with no actin overlap.
I band
Actin only — the light band either side of the Z disc.

During contraction the filaments slide but do not shorten, so only the bands that measure overlap change (Plate 1.4):

Band widths during contraction (Plate 1.4 · slide 9)
BandContainsDuring contraction
A bandMyosin (± actin overlap)Unchanged — myosin length is fixed
I bandActin onlyNarrows — actin slides into the A band
H zoneMyosin onlyNarrows / disappears — actin overlaps the centre
Label Key — Sarcomere in contraction
Z discs move inward
The sarcomere shortens as the Z discs are pulled toward the M line.
I band & H zone shrink
These measure non-overlap, so they narrow as filaments slide together.
A band constant
Confirms filaments slide rather than shorten — the key evidence for the sliding-filament theory.
Memory hook · which bands change

A band stays the sAme. The I band and H zone shrInk. If a band contains the fixed-length myosin end to end (A band), it can't change; the bands measuring gaps (I, H) close up.

§1.4One sarcomere — the proteins

Within the sarcomere sit the players of contraction (Plate 1.5): the contractile proteins that do the pulling and the regulatory proteins that decide when.

Label Key — Contractile & regulatory proteins
Myosin (thick filament)
Binds actin and performs the power stroke that pulls the thin filament.
Actin (thin filament)
Binds myosin during contraction; at rest its binding sites are blocked.
Tropomyosin
A regulatory protein that obstructs the myosin-binding sites on actin at rest.
Troponin
Controls tropomyosin; when calcium binds troponin it changes shape and pulls tropomyosin aside.
Reasoning · why muscle needs a molecular 'safety catch'

Actin and myosin will bind spontaneously — so a resting muscle needs something actively stopping them, or it could never relax. Tropomyosin is that catch, lying over actin's binding sites; troponin is the trigger that releases it, but only when calcium appears. This is the whole logic of the next two sections: contraction is really just calcium removing the safety catch.

R Recall checklist — structure
  • Sheaths — epimysium (whole muscle) · perimysium (fascicle) · endomysium (fibre); all merge into the tendon.
  • Fibre — myofibrils + T-tubules (carry AP inward) + SR (calcium store) + mitochondria/glycogen (fuel).
  • Sarcomere — Z disc (actin, edge) to Z disc; M line (myosin, middle); A band (overlap), H zone (myosin only), I band (actin only).
  • Contraction — A band unchanged; I band & H zone narrow (filaments slide, don't shorten).
  • Proteins — contractile (myosin, actin); regulatory (tropomyosin blocks, troponin + Ca releases).
§2Neuromuscular junction · LO2

The neuromuscular junction

The one-way, always-on switch from nerve to muscle — and the many ways to jam it.

§2.1Neural control

Skeletal muscle is driven by the somatic motor neurons — myelinated neurons running from the CNS to the muscle (Plate 2.1). Each axon's terminal branches innervate one muscle fibre each, and the effect is always excitatory, via the neurotransmitter acetylcholine (ACh).

Label Key — Somatic motor pathway
Somatic motor neuron
Myelinated; runs directly from CNS to skeletal muscle (no ganglionic relay).
Axon terminal branches
Each branch supplies one muscle fibre.
Acetylcholine (ACh)
The neurotransmitter released — its effect on skeletal muscle is always excitatory.
Nicotinic ACh receptor
On the muscle — where ACh acts.
Reasoning · why 'always excitatory' matters

Unlike the autonomic system (which can excite or inhibit its targets), a somatic motor neuron can only ever tell a muscle to contract — there is no 'relax' signal sent to the fibre. Relaxation happens only when the nerve stops firing. That single fact explains why anything blocking the NMJ (§2.4–2.6) causes weakness/paralysis, never over-contraction from the muscle side.

§2.2The junction — two halves

The NMJ has a neural half and a muscular half (Plate 2.2): the axon terminal of the motor neuron (which stores ACh in vesicles), and the motor end plate of the muscle fibre — a region packed with a high density of ACh receptors.

Label Key — NMJ components
Axon terminal (neuro-)
Distal end of the motor neuron; stores ACh in synaptic vesicles.
Motor end plate (muscular)
The specialised patch of sarcolemma with a high density of ACh receptors.
Synaptic cleft
The gap ACh diffuses across.
Skeletal muscle fibre
The target the signal is being handed to.

§2.3The receptor & how the signal crosses

The receptor is a ligand-gated ion channel — the nicotinic ACh receptor (nAChR) — and it is non-specific, passing both Na⁺ and K⁺ (Plate 2.3). Because Na⁺ influx exceeds K⁺ efflux, the net effect is depolarisation of the end plate.

Label Key — NMJ transmission & channel
ACh release
An action potential opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels in the terminal; Ca²⁺ triggers ACh-vesicle release into the cleft.
Ligand-gated nAChR
Opens when ACh binds — it is gated by a chemical (ligand), not by voltage.
Non-specific cation channel
Passes both Na⁺ and K⁺.
Na⁺ influx > K⁺ efflux
The net inward current depolarises the end plate — the end-plate potential that triggers the muscle action potential.
Reasoning · why one channel passes two ions yet still depolarises

The nAChR is a simple pore that both Na⁺ and K⁺ can cross. At rest the cell is far from Na⁺'s equilibrium but near K⁺'s, so opening the pore drives a much larger Na⁺ influx than K⁺ efflux. The imbalance is the whole point: a crude non-selective channel still produces a clean depolarisation because the electrochemical gradients are lopsided.

§2.4Modulation by drugs

Because the whole system funnels through one receptor, drugs that hit the nAChR have dramatic, opposite effects (slide 15):

Drugs acting at the nAChR
NicotineMuscle relaxants (curariform)
ContextCigarette smoking, vapingSurgical anaesthesia
MechanismBinds and activates nAChR → excess depolarisationBinds and inhibits nAChR → no depolarisation
Effect on muscleContraction; excess → prolonged depolarisation → paralysis; chronic use → desensitisationRelaxation
Clinical · why relaxants are used in surgery

Curariform drugs (the descendants of arrow-poison curare) block the nAChR so the muscle cannot be told to contract — giving the controlled paralysis needed for intubation and abdominal surgery. Their action is a live demonstration of §2.1: block the only 'on' switch and the muscle simply goes slack.

§2.5Modulation by bacterial neurotoxins

Two Clostridium toxins attack the pathway at different points, causing opposite paralyses (slide 16):

Botulinum vs tetanus toxin
Botulinum toxinTetanus toxin
BacteriumClostridium botulinumClostridium tetani
MechanismInhibits ACh release from the axon → no depolarisationInhibits inhibitory interneurons in the CNS → excess depolarisation ('disinhibition')
EffectFlaccid paralysis / relaxation (botulism)Spastic paralysis / contraction (tetanus)
Clinical · Botox — a poison put to work

Botulinum toxin's ability to shut off ACh release is used deliberately (Botox®) to relax overactive muscles or glands: migraine, overactive bladder, strabismus (squint) and blepharospasm (eyelid spasm), as well as cosmetically. Tetanus is the mirror image — by removing the CNS's braking interneurons it causes disinhibition, so motor neurons fire unchecked (lockjaw, whole-body rigidity).

Memory hook · botulinum vs tetanus

Botulinum → Body goes floppy (flaccid, blocks ACh release). Tetanus → Tense/rigid (spastic, blocks inhibition). Same family, opposite ends.

§2.6Myasthenia gravis

The classic NMJ disease (Plate 2.4): an autoimmune destruction of the nAChR. With fewer working receptors, the muscle's sensitivity to ACh falls, so contraction is reduced.

Label Key — Myasthenia gravis
Ptosis / facial weakness
Drooping eyelids and facial weakness — a common presentation; note it worsens later in the day.
Autoimmune loss of nAChR
Antibodies destroy the receptors, so ACh has fewer targets to act on.
Reduced response to ACh
Less depolarisation per nerve impulse → weaker contraction.
Clinical · why the treatment is an AChE inhibitor

The name decodes the disease — my- (muscle) -asthenia (weakness) gravis (severe) — weakness that worsens with exertion and through the day as the few remaining receptors tire. Management uses an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (e.g. neostigmine): by delaying ACh breakdown in the cleft, it leaves more ACh available to find the surviving receptors — treating the shortage of working receptors by boosting the transmitter, not replacing the receptor.

R Recall checklist — neuromuscular junction
  • Somatic motor neurons — myelinated, one fibre per terminal branch, always excitatory via ACh.
  • NMJ = axon terminal (stores ACh) + motor end plate (dense nAChR).
  • nAChR — ligand-gated, non-specific (Na⁺ & K⁺); Na⁺ influx > K⁺ efflux → depolarisation.
  • Nicotine activates (excess → paralysis/desensitisation); curariform relaxants block → relaxation.
  • Botulinum blocks ACh release → flaccid; tetanus blocks inhibition → spastic.
  • Myasthenia gravis — autoimmune loss of nAChR; treat with an AChE inhibitor (neostigmine).
§3Contraction & relaxation · LO3

The sliding-filament theory

Calcium removes the safety catch; myosin walks the actin in; ATP lets go.

Now the parts move. The sequence is: excitation (get calcium out), contraction (myosin pulls), and relaxation (put calcium back). Watch calcium and ATP — they are the two currencies of the whole process.

§3.1Excitation–contraction coupling

How does an electrical signal at the membrane release calcium deep inside? Through a mechanical relay in the T-tubule (Plate 3.1):

Label Key — E–C coupling
ACh → depolarisation
ACh opens nAChRs → the end plate depolarises → a muscle action potential.
AP down the T-tubule
The action potential propagates deep into the fibre along the T-tubule.
DHP receptor (voltage sensor)
In the T-tubule membrane; senses the voltage change and mechanically...
...opens the RyR on the SR
The ryanodine receptor calcium channel on the SR opens.
Ca²⁺ into the sarcoplasm
Calcium floods out of the SR store into the cytosol — the trigger for contraction.
Reasoning · why the DHP–RyR pair is the linchpin

The action potential is electrical and the calcium store is a separate membrane — something must couple them. The DHP receptor physically touches the RyR: when the DHP receptor feels the voltage change, it tugs the RyR open. This direct mechanical link is why the response is instant and why it is called excitation–contraction coupling — it is the hinge between the electrical (§2) and mechanical (below) halves of the story.

§3.2Contraction — the cross-bridge cycle

With calcium now in the sarcoplasm, the cross-bridge cycle runs (Plate 3.2):

Label Key — Cross-bridge cycle
ATP hydrolysis → cross-bridge
Myosin splits ATP and 'cocks' — it is now energised and reaches toward actin.
Ca²⁺ binds troponin
Calcium binds troponin, which pulls tropomyosin off the binding sites.
Tropomyosin uncovers site
Actin's myosin-binding sites are now exposed; myosin attaches.
Pi release → power stroke
Releasing inorganic phosphate triggers the power stroke — myosin pivots and pulls actin toward the M line.

The result at the whole-sarcomere level is the sliding-filament theory (Plate 3.3): the filaments do not change length — they slide past one another. Myosin ratchets actin toward the M line ~10 nm per stroke, the Z discs are drawn inward, and the sarcomere shortens.

Label Key — Sliding filaments
Filaments slide, not shorten
Actin and myosin keep their length — they simply overlap more.
Myosin pulls actin to the M line
Each power stroke moves actin ~10 nm; many cycles produce visible shortening.
Z discs move inward
Because actin is anchored to the Z disc, pulling actin in pulls the Z discs together → the sarcomere (and muscle) shortens.
Memory hook · the cycle in four beats

Cock (ATP split) → Catch (Ca frees actin, myosin binds) → Pull (Pi out, power stroke) → Release (new ATP). No ATP, no release — remember that for rigor mortis.

§3.3Relaxation

Relaxation is not passive — it costs ATP to undo the cycle and to put the calcium back (Plate 3.4):

Label Key — Relaxation
ADP released → rigor state
After the power stroke myosin is tightly bound to actin — the rigor state.
ATP binds myosin → detaches
A fresh ATP binding to myosin breaks the cross-bridge (stops the attachment).
Ca²⁺ pumped back to SR
The SR Ca-ATPase (SERCA) actively returns calcium to the store.
Tropomyosin re-covers the site
With calcium gone, tropomyosin slides back over actin — the safety catch is reset.
Reasoning · why relaxation needs ATP just like contraction

It is a common trap to think ATP only powers the pull. In fact ATP is needed to let go (it detaches myosin from actin) and to pump calcium back into the SR against its gradient. So a muscle with no ATP is stuck attached and flooded with calcium — which is exactly rigor mortis (§3.4).

§3.4Duration & rigor mortis

How long a contraction lasts depends on three things: stimulation at the NMJ, calcium in the sarcoplasm, and ATP availability. Remove them permanently and you get the ultimate failure to relax — rigor mortis (rigor = stiffness, mortis = of death).

Rigor mortis — why the body stiffens after death (slide 23)
CauseDeterminant
SR breaks downCalcium leaks into the sarcoplasm → binds troponin → cross-bridges form
Oxygen deprivation, glycolysis exhaustedNo ATP produced → ATP cannot bind myosin → cross-bridges cannot separate
What changes the timing of rigor
Rigor comes on soonerRigor is delayed
Warm temperatures; physical/emotional exertion (cadaveric spasm); low muscle mass (children, elderly); illnessCold temperatures; increased adiposity
Clinical / forensic · rigor mortis is §3 running out of fuel

Rigor mortis is the cross-bridge cycle frozen mid-step. At death the SR fails and leaks calcium (so cross-bridges keep forming), while no ATP is made (so they can never detach) — the muscle locks stiff. It is a direct, morbid proof that ATP is required for relaxation, and its timing (faster when warm or after exertion, slower when cold) helps forensic estimation of time of death.

R Recall checklist — contraction & relaxation
  • E–C coupling — AP down T-tubule → DHP receptor opens RyR → Ca²⁺ out of SR.
  • Cross-bridge cycle — ATP cocks myosin; Ca-troponin frees actin; Pi release = power stroke; ADP off = rigor.
  • Sliding filament — filaments slide (not shorten); myosin pulls actin ~10 nm/stroke; Z discs move in; sarcomere shortens.
  • Relaxation — ATP detaches myosin; Ca-ATPase pumps Ca²⁺ back to SR; tropomyosin re-covers actin.
  • Duration depends on NMJ stimulation, sarcoplasmic Ca²⁺, and ATP; rigor mortis = Ca leak + no ATP → cross-bridges locked.
